The Vārāhopaniṣad.
"May He protect us both"—this is the Peace mantra.
Chapter One.
Regarding the conceptual enumerations of the principles (*tattva-saṃkhyā-vikalpa*):
Now, the great sage Ṛbhu performed austerities for twelve years according to the divine measure. At the conclusion of that period, the Blessed One appeared in the form of a boar. He...

He said, "Arise, arise! Choose a boon. He arose and, having paid homage to him, said: "O Blessed One, whatever is desired by those who have desires, I do not ask for that from you even in a dream. [I seek] all the Vedas, Śāstras, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and the entire network of sciences."
"All the gods, beginning with Brahmā, have declared that liberation comes from knowing your true form.
Therefore, please speak the Brahma-vidyā which reveals your form," he said. "So be it," replied the Blessed One in the form of a boar.
Some proponents maintain that there are twenty-four principles;
some hold that there are thirty-six principles, and others that there are ninety-six.
I shall declare their sequence; listen with an attentive mind. (p. 465) [Commentary:
The venerable Varāhopaniṣad is the embodiment of indivisible bliss, known through realization.
I worship the feet of Rāmacandra, renowned as Tripādanārāyaṇa.

Indeed, this Varāhopaniṣad, which is a division of the Kṛṣṇayajurveda, stands preeminent; it reveals the ninety-six principles (*tattva*) while being intent on manifesting the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), and it culminates in the Turyaturya—the meaning of the Praṇava as the non-dual Brahman. Of this [Upaniṣad]...

A commentary is now begun from this very brief text. This narrative, consisting of questions and answers between Ṛbhu and Varāha (or Nidāgha and Ṛbhu), concerning [the fruits of] austerity, celibacy, the grace of the deities, and so forth, is intended for the purpose of praising the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).

At the beginning, he introduces the narrative with the word "atha" (now). He performed penance; that is, he practiced such exceedingly fierce austerity. He appeared before him; that is, he manifested himself in his presence. Having thus manifested, and desiring to bestow the fruit of the penance performed by him, he (the Lord) spoke. Having heard these words of the Blessed One in this manner—

He arose and said, "What is it? [The other replied,] "O Blessed One. When asked again, "Desiring what else do you perform this austerity?", he said, "All of this. They say that all bondage arises from ignorance of Your form, and liberation comes from knowledge of Your form. Having accepted the question posed by Ṛbhu, [the Lord said], "So be it."

Since, in the beginning, if there is an absence of thorough knowledge regarding the extent of reality as distinct from oneself, the disciple's intellect will not proceed toward the reality that is one's own nature alone; therefore, he explains the extent of reality as distinct from oneself with the word "four" (catur). || 1 ||
The twenty-four principles consist of the five organs of knowledge, namely hearing, touch, sight, and so forth. || 2 ||
The five organs of action are speech, hands, feet, and so forth, in their respective order;
likewise, there are the five vital breaths beginning with prāṇa, as well as the five [objects] beginning with sound. (3)
The intellect (manas), the faculty of cognition (buddhi), the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), and the mind (citta)— these four,
together with the twenty-four principles, are what the knowers of Brahman understand.
Regarding the question "What is that?", [the text says] "knowledge," etc. (2.4).
p. 466) There are thirty-six principles (*tattva*):
these aforementioned principles together with the five elements made by quintuplication (*pañcīkṛta*), namely earth, water, fire, air, and space. (5)
The wise know the three bodies to be the gross, the subtle, and the causal;
and likewise, the three states to be waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
In total, the sages know that there are thirty-six principles (tattvas).
To the question "Which are these thirty-six principles?", [the author replies] with the words "by these" (etair), etc. (vv. 5–6).
One should join the ninety-six principles together with the previously mentioned groups of principles.
There are six modifications of existence: it is born and it also grows;
transformation, decay, and destruction—these they know as the six modifications of existence. (8)
Hunger, thirst, sorrow, delusion, old age, and death—these are declared to be the six waves. Now, I shall describe to you the six sheaths.
Understand that skin, blood, flesh, fat, marrow, and bone, as well as desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy, are likewise [composed of these elements]. 10.
These are the six enemies, as well as the Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña—the triad of individual souls—and the three qualities: sattva, rajas, and tamas. (11)
It is taught that there are three types of karma: those already begun (*prārabdha*), those yet to come (*āgāmin*), and those accumulated (*arjita*).
There are five [functions]: speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure. (12)
Volition, determination, self-conceit, and ascertainment;
joy, compassion, loving-kindness, and equanimity—this is the tetrad. (13)
The guardians of the quarters, Vāta, Arka, Pracetas, the Aśvins, Vahni, Indra, Upendra, Mṛtyu, as well as Candra, the four-faced one (Brahmā), Rudra, Kṣetrajña, and Īśvara. || 14 ||
In total, ninety-six categories of principles (tattvas) have been proclaimed.
To the question "Which are these ninety-six principles?", [the answer is] "by those previously mentioned" (verse 7.14).

Liberation comes only from devotion to the Blessed One who transcends all principles; this is the stainless distinction between this [devotion] and the previously mentioned collection of principles. (15)
Those who worship me in my form as the Boar with true devotion become liberated from ignorance and its effects; they attain liberation while still living.
To the question, "Among those principles (tattvas) mentioned, what are you like? What is the fruit of your knowledge? he says:
"The aforementioned... (verses 15–16).

Those who know the ninety-six principles, for whom the fruit is the knowledge of reality, are liberated regardless of which stage of life they are devoted to—whether they wear matted hair, have a shaven head, or keep a topknot; of this there is no doubt. (17)
Thus it is said.

He states the fruit of the knowledge of the distinguished reality: "He who... The ninety-six principles accepted by the Sāṃkhya are subsumed within the thirty-six principles accepted by the Śaivas, and those [thirty-six] are, in turn, subsumed within the twenty-four principles accepted by certain followers of the Vedānta.

...are included. Furthermore, even those [categories] are included within the single reality of *māyā* which is distinct from oneself (*svātiriktamāyaikatattva*), because everything is an effect of *māyā*.

Since the reality of *māyā* distinct from oneself is of the nature of an absolute non-existence (*niṣpratiyogikābhāvarūpa*), nothing but the non-dual reality of Brahman (*niṣpratiyogikabrahmatattvamātra*) remains.
Thus ends the meaning of the established conclusions of all Vedānta. The word "iti" indicates the conclusion of the chapter.
Thus ends the first chapter.
The second chapter:
The attainment of the fourfold means.
"O Blessed One, you are the great yogi named Ṛbhu; please teach me the most excellent knowledge of Brahman concerning the Lord of Ramā in His form as a boar. (1)
Thus questioned, the Blessed One, the destroyer of the suffering of his devotees, said:
"By means of the dharma of one's own caste and stage of life, through austerity, and by pleasing the guru... (2)
The means for the accomplishment of men consists of the fourfold set beginning with dispassion:
the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal, and detachment from what is seen here and what is heard of in the hereafter. (3)
The perfection of the six qualities beginning with tranquility (śama) constitutes the desire for liberation; one should practice that.
Having thus understood the reality of Brahman in a general way, the sage, desiring to know the reality of Brahman clearly along with its means, asks the Blessed One—thus it is said:

"Rbhu," thus [it is said]. (1) To the question "What did he say? he first states that the practice of the means must be performed: "One's own caste... (2). To the question "What is that fourfold means to be practiced? he says: "The eternal... Brahma alone is eternal.
The discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal (*nityānityaviveka*) is the realization that everything other than Brahman is impermanent.

Dispassion toward this world and the next (*ihāmutravairāgya*) is the absence of desire for things such as garlands, sandalwood paste, and women in this life, and for enjoyments such as those in heaven in the next life, just as one feels toward vomit, urine, and excrement. (3) p. 469)

Tranquility, self-control, withdrawal, forbearance, faith, and concentration constitute the perfection of the sixfold set beginning with tranquility. Tranquility is the restraint of the internal organs;
self-control is the restraint of the external organs; withdrawal is the renunciation of all ritual actions.

*Titikṣā* is the endurance of dualities such as cold and heat; *śraddhā* is faith in the words of the scriptures and the teacher; *samādhāna* is one-pointedness of mind; and *mumukṣā* is the desire to be liberated from the delusion of being other than the Self. The meaning is that by practicing these four means in this manner, one becomes a master of the senses.
Only one who knows Brahman as the Self has accomplished all that is to be done;
having thus conquered the senses, he should abandon the notion of "mine" everywhere.
Having attained the rare human state and even within that, the male form, one should abandon the notion of "I" in Me, who am the witness-consciousness.

And the state of being a Brahmin belongs to Mahāviṣṇu through the hearing of the Vedānta and other means; His form is beyond the castes and stages of life, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.
He who does not know this is ignorant; when will he be liberated?
[The text] says "Thus" (evam) to indicate that one should cultivate the realization of Brahman alone, preceded by the renunciation of everything other than Brahman.
Thus, having resorted to a body such as that of a Brāhmaṇa, which is a means for knowledge—whosoever...

When does one who does not know the reality of his own self become liberated? He says: "Never"—meaning it is difficult to attain. (5) The manifest symbol (*vyaktaliṅga*) of Mahāviṣṇu is the state of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) produced by the hearing of Vedānta and other means; the unmanifest symbol (*avyaktaliṅga*) means that which transcends the castes and stages of life (*ativarṇāśrama*). (6)
The self has the nature of bliss;
"I myself am bliss, nothing else; if it were anything else, that would not be bliss at all. (7)
Nothing is dear for my sake; rather, it is dear in itself for my sake. May I always exist as the object of another's love. (8)
O Lord of Sages, he who perceives "May I become [Brahman]" is myself, Viṣṇu.

He declares that the state of being the sole object of all love belongs to his own Self alone—by saying "I. I am none other than the supreme bliss of Brahman, which is the inner self (pratyak) through its non-difference from the Supreme. It is nothing else.

Because anything other than Brahman must be sought; for if, in reality, there were something else, then that Brahman would not be non-relative bliss. This is because of the scriptural teaching that the nature of the Infinite Brahman (*bhūman*) is exclusively non-relative bliss, as stated in the text: "That which is the Infinite is bliss" (*yo vai bhūmā tat sukham*). 7. For this very reason:

That alone which is for my sake is happiness; that which is not for my sake cannot possibly be happiness. If it is argued that even what is for my sake does not become dear, [we reply] no; the meaning is that it becomes dear by its very nature. I am he who knows his own self as being of the nature of happiness.
Viṣṇu says: "Not so. The meaning is: it is not that I should not exist as the nature of undifferentiated bliss; rather, I must certainly exist as such. || 8 ||
The self-luminosity of the Self is not expressed by the statement "I am light," because that [statement] is dependent solely upon the manifestation [of light].
How could that which is not self-luminous touch the Self, which is self-luminous?
Those who know with perfect certainty that [Self] shines by itself and is without support— || 10 ||

For it is my firm conviction that they are indeed perfected in consciousness. Since it is pure existence (*sattāmātratvāt*), he says "not" [in the negation], because that which is pure existence is itself self-luminous Brahman. He does not see that which shines forth as "I am the light."

Its essential nature is pure luminosity (prakāśamātra). Because it devours non-luminosity, contact with non-luminosity is not possible; this is the meaning. Thus, he says "svayam" (by itself), implying: "I consider those who regard the Self as self-luminous to have accomplished all that was to be done. || 10 ||
The Self is distinct from its own māyā and its effects; apart from one's own full Self, there exist no such things as the world, individual souls, or the Lord. (11)
The non-existent and illusion do not exist, and I am distinct from them;
[ignorance] consists of the blinding darkness of nescience, characterized by karma, dharma, and so forth. (12)
The self-luminous Self does not deserve to be touched by "me.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dṛṣṭi*), nothing exists apart from oneself. If, however, it were to exist from the perspective of one who lacks self-knowledge (*svājña-dṛṣṭi*), then he says—referring to himself—that from the perspective of one who possesses self-knowledge (*svajña-dṛṣṭi*), he is distinct from that: "I am [the Self]. (11)
He says this because one might think that even though You are distinct from what is other than oneself, You could still be touched by that which is other than oneself: "By ignorance...
[The state of Brahman belongs] to the knower of the Self as Brahman; the nature of Brahman is the Self, the witness of all, who is distinct from the castes and stages of life. || 13 ||
Perceiving all this as being of the nature of Brahman, one becomes Brahman oneself;
for all that appears is the supreme state, whose very form is light.
Perceiving [the truth] through the authority of Vedānta, one is liberated immediately;
for knowledge is the sublater of the notion that the body is the self, just as the knowledge that the body is not the self sublates the notion that the body is the self. 15.
He in whom [this realization] exists within himself alone is liberated even against his will.

He who knows the inwardly shining Self as Brahman becomes Brahman itself, non-different from the inward Self; thus he says: "All... (verse 13). There is no object of illumination apart from the light [of consciousness].

He says that the knower is liberated from the state of being an object of appearance: "That which appears... (14). He says that thus the one of perfect knowledge is himself liberated: "The body... (15).
For the knower of the Self, there is an absence of bondage through karma;
[he attains] that which is characterized by truth, knowledge, and fullness of bliss, beyond darkness.
How could one who constantly perceives the bliss of Brahman—witnessing the three abodes and characterized by existence, consciousness, bliss, and so forth—be bound by karma? (17)

He states that for one who perceives the Self, there is no possibility of bondage through karma because the referent indicated by the words "you" and "I" is unattached to all defects— this is expressed in the verse beginning with "satya" (verse 16).
He states that non-attachment is the cause for the absence of the bondage of karma in one's own self: "The three abodes... (verse 17).
The difference between the vision and the state of being of the ignorant and the wise:
the eye of knowledge beholds that which is all-pervading, Being-Consciousness-Bliss. (18)
One whose eye of knowledge is obscured cannot perceive the radiant Sun, just as a blind man cannot;
that very Brahman is pure consciousness, characterized by true awareness. (19)
Thus, through the complete realization of Brahman alone, a mortal becomes immortal;
that Brahman is non-dual bliss, devoid of qualities, the mass of pure existence and consciousness. (20)
Having realized the nature of one's own self as pure consciousness—omnipresent, eternal, complete, and imperishable bliss—one does not fear anything whatsoever. (21)
"Brahman alone is manifest, there is nothing else"—such is the conviction of those who know Brahman;
to the ignorant, the world consists of a flood of suffering, but to the wise, it consists of bliss.
The world is blind to the blind, but it is light for those with clear vision.
One who possesses the eye of knowledge perceives the Self as unattached to everything;
however, one whose eye is the ignorance of their own self does not perceive the radiant Self, like a person blind by day. Thus he says:
"All-pervading" (sarvagam) || 18 || He states that one who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself, just as it is:
"Consciousness" (prajñānam) || 19 || He states that the knower of Brahman does not fear anything from any source: "That" (tat) || 20 ||
To the question, "What is the state of those who know Brahman and are free from fear? he says: "Pure consciousness alone" (cinmātram). || 21 ||
He says that one who is ignorant perceives what is grasped by his own cognition as being contrary [to reality]: "of the ignorant," [verse 22].
In reality, there is neither bondage nor liberation for the Self within me, who am infinite, existence-consciousness-bliss, and in the form of the Boar. (23)
When [the Self] abides [in its true state], there would be non-duality; who then is bound, and who is liberated?
For the own-nature of all embodied beings is always pure consciousness alone. (24)
The aggregate of the body and so forth is not at all an object of perception like a jar;
rather, this entire world of moving and non-moving things appears as something other than one's own self. (25)
Having realized it as being nothing but one's own self, contemplate "I am that.
One experiences one's own true nature by oneself; there is no object of enjoyment separate from itself.
If there is that which has the nature of existence, it is Brahman alone characterized by existence;
one endowed with the knowledge of Brahman perceives the entire world as such.
Even while seeing, he never sees anything as separate from his own self;
through the thorough knowledge of my true nature, he is not bound by actions. 28.
He who [knows] that which is devoid of body, senses, and so forth; the witness of all; whose sole realization is the ultimate reality; whose nature is bliss; and who is self-luminous. || 29 ||
He who knows everything through his own experience as being his very own nature—he is wise; he indeed is to be known. "I am that"; O friend, become established in that reality.
Therefore, the experience of phenomenal expansion is not eternal,
whereas the experience of the realization of one's own true nature is indeed eternal; perceiving this thus, the one who possesses complete knowledge—
He is neither liberated from bondage, nor indeed bound at all. || 31 ||

In reality, because I am non-dual and without a counterpart (*niṣpratiyogikādvitīya*), no one can possibly be bound or liberated; thus he says: "The Infinite" (*ananta*). (23) What bondage could there be in the state of non-duality?
In accordance with the Śruti, "Consciousness alone is indeed consciousness alone," one's own true nature is nothing but pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). It is not...

He says it is "other"—namely, one's own essential nature (svasvarūpa). || 24 || He says that one should contemplate the body and so forth, which are distinct from oneself, as being nothing but oneself (svamātra)—namely, "of one's own self" (svātmanaḥ). || 25 || There is simply nothing apart from oneself. If there is the delusion that such a thing exists, then he says that even that existence is Brahman—namely, "one's own" (sva). || 26 || One who knows oneself.

He says "Brahman" [in verse 27] to show that one does not perceive what is other than oneself as being other, but rather perceives it as being nothing but oneself. To the question, "When there is bondage through karma, how can one perceive in this way?
he says "Me" [in verse 28]. Having raised the doubt, "Even when the body and so forth exist, why is one not bound in this way? [the text proceeds].
He says "yaḥ" (he who) to show that he who perceives the Self as distinct from that [body] would be none other than himself: "yaḥ."

29-30 || Thus, for one who has attained my state, there is no experience of the manifold world of non-self apart from the experience of one's own Self. He says "Therefore" (ataḥ) [in verse 31] to show that for the yogi who experiences his own Self in this way, the delusion of bondage and liberation does not exist. 31 ||

For the cessation of bondage, one should contemplate the Self as Brahman; he who meditates for even a moment upon Me—the witness of all, who dances through the contemplation of His own true nature—is liberated from all fetters. (32)
Salutations again and again to me alone, who abide within all beings, whose nature is the eternally liberated consciousness, and whose form is inward-facing awareness.
O Blessed One, you are indeed I; O Divine Being, I am indeed you.
To you who are the infinite I, and to me who am the conscious Self—to you and to me! || 34 ||
Salutations to me, the Supreme Lord; salutations to you, O Śiva!
What shall I do? Where shall I go? What shall I take up? What shall I abandon? (35)

Just as the entire universe was filled by me with the waters of the great dissolution (*mahākalpa*), so too he who abandons internal attachment, external attachment, and attachment to the self—he whose soul is withdrawn from all attachments—attains me; of this there is no doubt. (36)
He who always avoids association with people as one would a snake, and who, having abandoned desire and being free from passion,
regards sense-objects and the like as poisonous and fraught with dire consequences, [is truly wise].
In this world, I alone am Vāsudeva, the supreme swan.
This is truth, this is truth; this is declared here as the truth:
"I am the Truth, Brahman; nothing whatsoever exists apart from me. (38)
Anticipating the question, "What is the cause for the cessation of bondage? he says, "One's own [meditation]," namely, "meditation upon Me."
32 || He describes the method for contemplating Brahman as non-different from the inner self (pratyag-abhinna-brahmānusaṃdhāna): "All...
|| 33-34 || He also states his own changelessness and fullness: "What shall I do?
|| 35 || Regarding the point that all beings attain you alone because of your omnipresence—even though they have constantly attained me...

Those who are attached to what is other than themselves do not attain Me. In this regard, he says—beginning with "internally"—that whoever becomes free from attachment to both the internal and external attains Me alone. (36)
He states the means for abandoning attachment to what is other than one's own Self, as well as the fruit of that knowledge, in the verse beginning with "ahih" (37).
"I alone am Vāsudeva; this is the truth. There exists nothing other than me that is unreal, because everything other than me is merely sought after. Thus he says: "This... (verse 38).
Regarding the etymology of fasting (*upavāsa*), which serves as the means for attaining Brahman:
that which is the dwelling (*vāsa*) near (*upa*) the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is to be known as fasting; it is not the withering of the body. (39)
What is the use of the mere emaciation of the body for those lacking discernment?
For does a great serpent die simply by being struck upon an anthill? (40)
Regarding the question of what is the means for attaining the Brahman that is Truth, he says: "Upa... (verses 39–40).
The means to liberation while living is immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*).
If one knows "Brahman exists," that is merely mediate knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*);
if one knows "I am Brahman," that is called direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). (41)
From the moment the yogi knows his own self as absolute, from that time forward he becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 42 ||
The realization "I am Brahman" is the certain cause of liberation for the great-souled ones.
He describes the nature of indirect and direct knowledge [of Brahman] with the words: "It exists," etc. (41).
He states that one becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta) simultaneously with the arising of direct knowledge (aparokṣajñāna), beginning with the words "yasmin" (in which). || 42 ||
He states that the knowledge "I am always Brahman" is the cause of liberation: "I... [etc.].
The method for abandoning thoughts of the external and internal consists of two words for the sake of bondage and liberation: "mine" and "not mine. (43)
A living being is bound by the thought "this is mine," and is liberated by the thought "this is not mine.
One should not engage in external reflection, nor likewise in internal reflection.
Having completely abandoned all reflection, O sage, remain forever established in your own self.

He states that the presence or absence of the notions of "I" (ahaṃkāra) and "mine" (mamakāra) regarding the body and so forth are the causes of bondage and liberation—thus [he says]: "The two" (verse 43). He further states that the very abandonment of internal and external thought is the cause for the non-arising of the sense of "I" and so forth—thus [he says]: "External" (verse 44).
Meditation upon the Blessed One alone is the means for abandoning all other thoughts;
for the entire world is a mere construction of volition,
and the manifestation of the world consists in nothing but the construction of volition.
Abandon this mere conceptualization and, relying on the state free from conceptual construction, meditate upon my state within your heart. (45)
O high-minded one, spend your time becoming solely devoted to me—thinking of me, speaking of me, conversing with one another about me, and addressing me alone. (46)
"Consciousness alone exists here; this is consciousness-only and consists entirely of consciousness.
Contemplate thus: 'I am consciousness, these worlds are consciousness, and everything is consciousness. (47)
"Having brought passion to the state of passionlessness, remain forever untainted;

uprooting the volition that is the root of anxiety, take refuge in me, who am free from conceptual construction," he says—this is verse 45. He states the means for abandoning volition—this is verse 46: "meditation upon you... [end of fragment].
Regarding the question "of what kind? he says "consciousness" (cid), meaning that one should contemplate everything as being pure consciousness alone. || 47 ||
Attachment toward objects other than oneself.

Brahman alone, which transcends all conceptual constructions, should be contemplated, [remaining unaffected] by the karma produced by the causal factors such as the agent, which arise from ignorance. 48.
How can the lamp of self-knowledge produced by the Vedas be sublated, when it has abandoned the state of non-self and remains changeless throughout the existence of the world? (49)
Be intent solely upon the consciousness residing within through single-minded devotion;
the space within a jar and the space within a hut are both established in the great space.
Thus, within me, the space of consciousness, the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) were imagined;
that which was previously attributed to my self has likewise been discarded at the end.

p. 478) Those who discourse on Brahman declare, through discernment, that this is Māyā; when Māyā and its effects dissolve, there is neither the state of being the Lord nor the state of being a living soul. (52)

Therefore, I am pure consciousness alone, like the sky and devoid of limiting adjuncts; [it is I who appear] in the form of the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśvara), and so forth, as well as the nature of both the sentient and the insentient.
The creation, beginning with the act of seeing and ending with entry [into the body], is fashioned by the Lord;
the cycle of existence, beginning with the waking state and ending with liberation, is fashioned by the individual soul. (54)

Those beginning with the Triṇāciketa and ending with Yoga rely on the delusion regarding Īśvara; those beginning with Lokāyata and ending with Sāṃkhya rely on the delusion regarding the individual soul (jīva). || 55 ||
Therefore, those seeking liberation should not direct their minds toward the doctrines of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa);
rather, the reality of Brahman should be investigated with unwavering concentration. 56.
To the extent that they do not know the non-dual reality of Brahman, all of them are indeed deluded; for them, where is liberation, or where is happiness in this world? (57)
Since the staining by karma is unavoidable, one might ask: "How could I be free from stain? To this, he says:
"Through ignorance... (verse 48). Since the non-self exists, how can the knowledge of the Self alone arise?
To this, he says: "...would it be? (verse 50). [This is because] Māyā, which is the root of the conceptualization of the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (Īśa), and so forth, exists.

Regarding the question, "How may I become free from illusion (nirmāya)? he says, "And that which... (vv. 51–52), explaining that through inquiry into the root of illusion, Brahman—which is beyond illusion—becomes manifest.

Having abandoned the manifold conceptualizations such as the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), which are characterized by the definitions previously stated, he says that only the non-conceptual, non-dual Brahman should be constantly contemplated—beginning with "the individual soul" (*jīva*) and ending with "should be investigated with an unwavering mind. This [passage] has been explained in the *Mahopaniṣad*. Thus.
He states that those who do not know Brahman as the undivided single essence are indeed deluded: "Advitīya... (verse 57).

If Brahman, which is non-different from the inner self and transcends all states, were subject to the condition of being superior or inferior, what would that matter? For one who has awakened is certainly not affected by either the kingdom or the begging experienced in a dream. (58)
Sleep is said by the wise to be ignorance and the dissolution of the intellect;
how could there be sleep in Me, wherein ignorance and its effects have dissolved? (59)
This full blossoming of the intellect is proclaimed as "waking" (jāgara);
because it is devoid of modification and the like, waking does not exist for me.
The movement of the intellect within the subtle channels gives rise to the dream state;
in me, who am devoid of the property of movement, no dream exists.

Regarding the question of how the knowledge of the non-dual Brahman can arise when distinctions such as Śiva and the individual soul (jīva), or superior and inferior, exist, he refutes that with an illustration: "Superior... (verse 58).

To the question, "How can there be an experience of the bliss of the Fourth (turyānanda) for one who is veiled by the three states? he says: "Ignorance... etc. Here, *nidrā* refers to deep sleep (*suṣupti*). (Verses 59–61)
Through the knowledge of Brahman without distinction, the state of being Brahman occurs;
at the time of deep sleep, when all has dissolved and one is enveloped by darkness, one enjoys one's own nature as great bliss, free from the visible world. (62)
He who perceives everything without distinction because of its continuity with consciousness—he alone is the direct possessor of true knowledge; he is Śiva, he is Hari, he is Brahmā.
Thus, during the state of deep sleep (suṣupti) regarding the phenomenal world (prapañca) that is other than oneself;
he says "without distinction" (aviśeṣeṇa) [in verse 63] to show that the knower who is woven through all states of consciousness becomes consciousness itself.

(480) Contemplating the oneness of Brahman preceded by the dissolution of the world— this which is saṃsāra, an ocean of suffering, is either a long dream, or a prolonged delusion of the mind, or a vast kingdom of the imagination.
Rising from sleep, let one contemplate the single Brahman that persists until the end of sleep.
By dissolving the superimposed world,
our mind is conceived as being of the nature of the "I";
having slain the enemies, it falls from the host of the six teachers.
He becomes a scent-elephant, solitary and without equal. || 65 ||

He describes the state of the mind as being a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) through the cycle of the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep]—starting with the word "long" (*dīrgha*). The meaning is: "Know it to be an ocean of suffering. Since this is so, therefore, for the sake of its pacification, one should rise from sleep. To the question, "By what means should one contemplate that Brahman is one? he says: "Of that which is superimposed" (*āropitasya*). This is from the perspective of one who lacks self-knowledge (*svājña-dṛṣṭyā*).
By the dissolution of that which has been projected, the presiding principle of dissolution remains;

therein, the mind possessing an unfragmented form becomes my very own nature—this is the meaning. [One should destroy] the enemies who are the veils of Being-Consciousness-Bliss, or the sixfold group of foes such as desire and so forth, by means of the group [of means] from the sixfold collection of teachers.

Having struck down and eradicated [the enemies] with the sword of the six virtues beginning with tranquility (śama), through this destruction of the foes, the Self alone remains—like a scent-elephant (gandhadvīpa) or a rutting elephant that is solitary and peerless; this is the meaning.
The experience of the wise has as its object Brahman, which is non-different from the inner self;
let the body go to destruction this very day, and let the moon perish—
what difference does that make to me, whose nature is consciousness?
Whether the jar perishes or remains for a long time, there is indeed not the slightest difference in the space within the jar. || 66 ||
The slough of a snake, though devoid of life, remains fallen upon an anthill; the serpent does not regard it as himself. (67)
Thus, when false knowledge together with its cause has been destroyed by the fire-tuft of inward wisdom, one no longer identifies with the gross or the subtle body;
because his nature is defined by "not this, not this" (neti neti), he becomes bodiless.
Through scripture, the vision of ultimate reality may perish;
through direct perception, that which is capable of action perishes;
and through the destruction of *prārabdha* karma, the manifestation [of the world] perishes.
In this way, the self-illusion perishes in three ways.
When one's own state as Brahman is established, the condition of being a living soul (jīva) does not persist;
when the reality of non-duality is realized, latent impressions (vāsanā) cease to exist.
At the end of its commencement, the abandonment of the body occurs; in this way, everything is dissolved.
When it is said "it exists," the entire world becomes that Brahman, whose essence is Being. (71)
When it is said that "it shines," the entire universe is nothing but the manifestation of Brahman alone;
just as all water in a desert is merely the desert itself, so too, through self-inquiry, this entire triple world is pure consciousness alone. (72)
Ignorance itself does not exist; how then could there be the contingency of a world?
The discourse concerning the distinctions of individual soul, Lord, and teacher lies far beyond.
In that which is of the nature of a single, absolute, and pure consciousness, there is but one flavor.
I am indeed Brahman alone, the all-pervading perfection. || 73 ||
When the moon of awakening has its full form, yet its own splendor has been stolen by the Rāhu of delusion,
[what use are] rituals such as bathing, giving, and sacrifice?
It remains in vain until the time of liberation. || 74 ||
He says "Now" (adya) to show that the experience of the wise person who has attained my own nature occurs in this way.
Regarding this, the illustration is: "When the jar perishes. [Objection: Since the body of the wise person is still perceived, how can he be bodiless?
Anticipating this doubt, [the text continues]: "Indeed, for one who is truly bodiless, pleasure and pain do not touch. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.7)

In accordance with the scriptural statement "they touch," he provides an illustration to show that for one who has discriminated against the three bodies imagined by his own ignorance, the very state of being free from the notions of "self" and "mine" regarding those bodies is indeed bodilessness: "Like a snake sloughing its skin" (67). Through the knowledge (*jñāna*), realized knowledge (*vijñāna*), and perfect knowledge of reality (*samyaktattvajñāna*) born of the scriptures, one realizes that Māyā does not exist apart from Brahman; thus, having dispelled Māyā, one attains the state beyond Māyā (*māyā-nirmāya-pada*), simultaneously with that realization.
Even the three types of karma, beginning with those that have begun to bear fruit (*āgāmi*), along with their latent impressions (*savāsana*), are destroyed;

This is because of the knowledge produced by the scripture that "Brahman alone is real; there is nothing whatsoever apart from Brahman."

Through the vision of ultimate reality, the illusion is destroyed. Consequently, there occurs a non-attachment (*aśleṣa*) to future karma, which has as its locus an identity born from the delusion produced by that seed-portion. At that time, the conventional world appears as something separate from one's own self.

If the knowledge produced by scriptures previously studied becomes established in direct experience, it attains the status of *vijñāna*; consequently, that which was functionally efficient and empirical perishes.
Thereby, only the phenomenal (*prātibhāsika*) appears as distinct from one's own self. By that—

Even accumulated karma, which is rooted in innate identity, perishes. For the man of realization, however, prārabdha-karma is exhausted through experience; it does not perish at that moment because it has already begun to bear fruit. This is provided that his realization is endowed with firm experiential conviction.
One resorts to the state of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). By that, one resorts to the void-nature (*śūnyabhāva*) which appears as something separate from oneself due to its illusory manifestation.
Through that, even karma—which has been initiated by the gross aspect of *māyā*, the locus of the self born of action—is destroyed.

Simultaneous with the destruction of *prārabdha*, even the appearance of *māyā* perishes due to its emptiness. Thus, the meaning is that *māyā* is destroyed in three ways. Existence, manifestation, and loveliness, as well as form and name—this is the fivefold division.
The first three constitute the nature of Brahman; the latter two constitute the nature of the world.
Thus says the Śruti. To the objection that Brahman has name and form as its second [attribute], he says: "In the desert land" (marubhūmau) || 72 ||

73 || He says "bodha" etc., [to show] that fools, having imagined something separate from Brahman—which is free from any notion of being other than itself—vainly exert themselves for its pacification. 74 ||
The means of accomplishing samādhi is the continuous contemplation of the inner sound (nāda);
just as salt in water attains a state of equilibrium through union, so too the unification of the self and the mind is called samādhi. (75)
The renunciation of sense objects is difficult to attain; the vision of reality is difficult to attain;
and the innate state is difficult to attain without the compassion of a true guru. (76)
For the yogi who has awakened the power that has arisen and abandoned all karma without exception,
the innate state (sahajāvasthā) manifests of its own accord.
The fickleness of both the vital essence (rasa) and the mind is innate by nature;
when the essence is bound and the mind is bound, what on this earth cannot be accomplished? (78)

When swooned, it removes disease; when dead, it restores life itself; when bound, it bestows the power of moving through the sky; and when the mercury is within the mind, it grants the state of Brahman. (79)
The mind is the lord of the senses, but the vital breath (māruta) is the lord of the mind;
the dissolution of the vital breath is its lord—take refuge in that dissolution as your lord. 80.
Motionless and free from modification, the dissolution (*laya*) of yogis lives on;
with all volitions severed and all activities entirely ceased, this dissolution is something to be realized within oneself, beyond the reach of the mind and outside the domain of speech. (81)
Even while intent on observing objects one after another,
the yogi does not abandon the mind fixed on the vision of Brahman;
even though she has fallen under the sway of song, rhythm, tempo, and instrumental music, [the mind remains fixed].
Like a dancer, her mind is intent on guarding the primary jar placed upon her head. || 82 ||
Having abandoned all thought, one who desires the sovereignty of yoga should, with a vigilant mind, focus exclusively upon the sound (nāda). 83.
Thus [it is said].

He states, with an illustration, that "I am Brahman"—the oneness of Brahman and the mind—established through the awakening to the impossibility of anything other than oneself, is *samādhi*: "As in water... (75).
Thus, he says "it is difficult to attain" (durlabhaḥ) [verse 76] to show that the vision of reality arises through the glance of the Guru.
To the question, "In whom does this innate state arise?", he says: "arisen" (*utpanna*).

This refers to one for whom the awakening of the power of Kuṇḍalinī has arisen through proficiency in the practice of yoga conjoined with knowledge, and who possesses the awakening of the powers of non-inert action, knowledge, and will, [realizing] that nothing exists apart from Brahman.

Or [it refers] to one who possesses right knowledge and has awakened power. (77) Regarding those who believe that the mind exists as something distinct from Brahman, he states—with an illustrative example—that the movement and other activities of the mind are the cause of bondage and liberation, relying upon their perspective: p. 485) [He says: "The movement and so forth of the mind are the cause of bondage and liberation. [This is stated] with an illustrative example.

Regarding the phrase "of the rasa" (rasasya) [verses 78–79]: having sequentially dissolved the senses, mind, vital breaths, and so forth, one should take refuge in the thought "I am Brahman," which is the substratum for their dissolution; thus he says: "of the senses" (indriyāṇām) [verse 80].

As for the question, "What is this dissolution (laya) like?", the answer is: "motionless. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "utterly destroyed": the meaning is that by the word *laya*, Brahman—the substratum of dissolution—is denoted. (81) To the question, "Even though sense objects exist, why does the knower perceive the vision of Brahman as the substratum of their dissolution? he provides an answer supported by an illustration:

"Thus ends the eighth [verse]. He concludes the meaning of the chapter with the words "all," etc., stating that the Supreme Self—established through the awakening to the impossibility of delusion regarding anything other than oneself—is to be realized as nothing but one's own self (svāvaśeṣadhiyā).
For one who desires the sovereignty of Yoga, which is liberation (kaivalya), that [Self] allows no room for what is other than itself; thus it is a "river" (nada).
In this way, one should contemplate that the Nāda is indeed the Supreme Self alone, which is its own non-dual, peerless nature. || 83 ||
The word "iti" signifies the completion of the chapter.
Thus ends the second chapter.
The third chapter:
The experience of the non-dual Supreme Self.
Indeed, a single entity can never possess diverse natures;
therefore, I am truly undivided, for there is nothing whatsoever other than me. (1)
Whatever is seen or heard that is other than Brahman does not truly exist;
I am that Supreme Brahman—eternal, pure, liberated, one, indivisible, non-dual bliss, truth, consciousness, and infinite. || 2 ||
I am of the nature of bliss, undivided consciousness; I am beyond the supreme, the dense radiance of pure awareness.
Just as clouds do not touch the sky, [so am I untouched by the world].
The sufferings of saṃsāra do not touch me. || 3 ||
Know that all is happiness through the destruction of suffering, and all is of the nature of reality through the destruction of error;
it is indeed the nature of consciousness, endowed with manifestation.
Therefore, this form of mine is indivisible.
For there is no birth nor death, no going nor coming, no impurity nor purity, and no sensation; indeed,
everything shines forth as consisting of consciousness alone.
But for the supreme yogin, it is even more manifest. || 5 ||

Observing the doubt, "How can you be the non-correlative Supreme Self when multiplicity, which is your own correlative, exists?", the Lord reveals His own experience to establish His state as the non-correlative, non-dual Absolute: "Indeed not... (na hi).
Since it is so, therefore [the verse says]: || 1 || Regarding the statement "something other than oneself is seen and heard," he replies:
"is seen. Regarding the question "what kind of Brahman are you?", he replies: "eternal" || 2 ||
Because of the commonality of maintaining a body like that of a living being, you too would become a sufferer of the miseries of saṃsāra; therefore, he says:
"Ānanda... (3). He says: "Know me as the indivisible Being-Consciousness-Bliss" (saccidānandākhaṇḍa), stating: "All... (4).
He states that for one who possesses the yoga of non-differentiated knowledge, only my own form shines forth: "Indeed, there is no birth," and so on.

The meaning is that the yogi, realizing that there is no modification such as birth, death, going, or coming in me, his own Self, perceives me everywhere as the non-dual, absolute pure consciousness. || 5 ||

Take refuge in the vow of silence, realizing "I am always That"— the state of pure consciousness, the means for attaining which is the practice of silence; that state which is the Truth, a mass of consciousness, indivisible, non-dual, devoid of all objects of perception, free from affliction, stainless, and auspicious.

Free from birth and death, pleasure and pain, and far removed from caste, conduct, family, and lineage—that which is the cause of this world, which is an evolution of consciousness, is always "I"; take refuge in that silence. (7)

Full, non-dual, indivisible consciousness, devoid of the conceptualization of the world's manifoldness, that which is a portion of the peerless supreme awareness—always take refuge in the silence of "I am That. (8)

Observing him asking, "Since you are the Lord, it is logical that you are non-dual pure consciousness alone; but as for me, being a non-lord, please instruct me on the means to attain that state," the Blessed One instructs him on the means to attain his own true nature: "The Real" (satya), etc. (6–8).
The Blessed One’s nature as Being-Consciousness-Bliss exists because it is uncontradicted by anything and remains uniform throughout the three periods of time;
this state of being "Being" (sat-rūpatva) is eternally mine.
That which is unconditioned and eternal, which in deep sleep is beyond all pleasure—
this nature of being of the form of bliss is my constant state of bliss.

Having thus taught the means for attaining the true nature of the Sage, he establishes his own state as being existence-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda) for the sake of its firm consolidation, beginning with the verse "By what... (9–10).
Devotion to the Blessed One alone is the means to liberation;
for by the rays of the sun, even the most dense darkness of night is instantly destroyed.
The darkness that is the cause of dense existence cannot be dispelled by anything other than the light of the sun of Dharma. || 11 ||
By the remembrance of my feet and by worship,
a living being is indeed liberated from his own darkness;
for there is no other cause for the destruction of death and rebirth.
Apart from the remembrance of my feet, is there anything else? || 12 ||
If one were to praise the Creator of the Universe with the same devotion that a person seeking wealth praises a wealthy man out of desire for riches, who would not be liberated from bondage? (13)

He establishes with an illustration that no one is liberated without devotion, which is the cause for attaining my own state: "By the light of the sun... [it goes to destruction]. This means that without the light of the sun, it perishes.

11–12 || Just as someone, even if served by a king, may be released from poverty, so too, who would not be released from the delusion of being something other than the Self by worshiping Me? Thus he says: "With reverence" (ādareṇa). || 13 ||
Just as the world acts by itself in the presence of the sun,
so too does the entire universe act in my presence alone. 14.
Just as silver is imagined in mother-of-pearl through illusion, so too this world, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), consists of illusion and exists solely within me. 15.

Whether in the body of a caṇḍāla, in animals and so forth, in stationary objects, or in the form of Brahman, or in others situated according to their respective degrees of excellence—I am not otherwise [than that]. (16)

Just as the directions appear exactly as before even to one whose confusion regarding the directions has been destroyed, so too does the world appear to me, though it has been demolished by higher knowledge; for it is not truly there.
It is neither the body, nor the senses and vital breaths, nor the mind, intellect, or ego; it is neither the consciousness, nor indeed illusion, nor the world consisting of space and the rest. (18)
Neither an agent, nor an enjoyer, nor likewise one who causes enjoyment;
I am merely Janārdana, the Brahman that is pure consciousness, existence, and bliss. 19.
He says, "I alone am the cause of the engagement and disengagement of the world, beginning with those ignorant of their own Self" (verse 14):

*āditya* etc. [The meaning is: that which is other than Me is merely conceptualized within Me. He says, "I alone am the same even amidst the uneven" (verses 15–16): *śuktikāyām* etc. [The meaning is: it is conceptualized through my own ignorance.

He says, "Because of the knowledge of the Self, it does not appear," [beginning with] "vinaṣṭa" (perished). [Verse 17: "Even for one whose delusion regarding the directions has perished, when that delusion has ceased...
