The mind alone is the cause of saṃsāra;
just as the sun appears to be unsteady only because of the flickering water, so too does saṃsāra belong to the Self only through its connection with the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). 20.
For saṃsāra has its root in the mind; one should therefore purify it with effort.
Alas! What is this trust you place in the greatness of the mind? 21.
Where are the riches of kings, or where are the worlds of the brahmins? The wealth of former ages has departed, and the successions of creations have passed away. (22)
Tens of millions of Brahmins have passed away and kings have perished like dust;
even that sense of self-identity regarding the inner self persists due to the demonic nature of the learned as well. (23)
If even a learned person were of an *āsura* (demoniac) nature, his vision of reality would be fruitless. (p.

490) Let it be that for You, the Lord, there is an absence of body and so forth, because You are in fact of the nature of the undifferentiated Brahman. Regarding the question of what are the causes of bondage and liberation for individual souls (*jīvas*):
He says, "Because of the existence of that [in what is not that] and the non-existence of that [in what is not that]," referring to the phrase "of water" (jalasya).

|| 20 || Thus, when asked what the root of saṃsāra is, he says "the mind" (citta) in the phrase "of the mind. To one who, because the mind—the root of saṃsāra—exists, believes that everything conceptualized by it is real, he says "Alas! (hanta).

The meaning is that because the mind and its effects revive delusion, and because they are no longer seen as before once that [delusion] has departed, the conceptualization of the mind and its effects does not exist at all. (21–22) He says "And he... to show that if even for a wise person things appear in this way as if real, then his wisdom does not exist: "He who [perceives] in the non-self..."

That conceit of the self (*adhyātmābhimāna*), which arises from the notion of a self and is the domain of the ignorant—namely, the conceit of the body and the sense of "mine" regarding things other than oneself—is indeed a source of harm even for the learned. Why?
Because such conceit of self and possession toward the body and so forth is demonic in nature, being the work of the demonic. (23) [This refers to] the ignorant person.
Even for the learned, if their disposition is demonic (*āsura*), then the realization of reality they have acquired will be entirely fruitless. Thus says the Śruti:
"For the yogi who is satisfied by the nectar of knowledge and has accomplished all that was to be done..."
There is nothing whatsoever that remains to be done; if there were something to be done, one would not be a knower of reality.
Thus [it is said].
The experience of passion and other afflictions within what is not the self is the characteristic of the wise; for those passions that arise are consumed by the fire of discriminative knowledge. (24)
Just as they are burned at that very moment, how could there be any sprouting for them?
Just as one who is extremely skillful and intent on observing the faults of others [sees them clearly]. (25)
If that were so, who among the wise would not be liberated from bondage? Even one who does not know the Self, though unliberated, still craves a web of supernatural powers.
O Lord of Sages, one attains [the goal] through the application of substances, mantras, rituals, time, and logic;
this is not the domain of the knower of the Self, for the knower of the Self perceives only the Self.
Satisfied within the self by means of the self, one does not pursue ignorance;
whatever worldly phenomena there may be, they know them to be composed of ignorance.
How indeed does one who knows the Self, having abandoned ignorance, immerse himself in those [mantras], when substances, mantras, rituals, times, and methods grant the success of the virtuous? (29)
No particular desires assist in the attainment of the state of the Supreme Self; rather, it is the cessation of all volitions that is designated as the arising of self-realization. (30)
How can he desire spiritual accomplishment, and how can he be worthy of it while being without mind?
Thus [it is said].

He states that there is no possibility of regrowth for that demonic state—which is to be cultivated by the ignorant—once it has been consumed by the fire of knowledge at the very moment the state of a wise person arises, leaving nothing but ashes:
"Having produced... (verse 24). If one's own demonic nature has arisen like the searching out of others' faults, then who indeed [is not affected]?

He says "is liberated" and explains with the words "just as" (yathā). || 25 || One who does not know the Self attains powers such as atomization (*aṇimā*) through the appropriate means for them; however, one who knows the Self, considering those [powers] to be effects of the non-Self, desists from them. He says "one who does not know the Self" to show that the very desire for them does not arise in him. || 26–27 ||

"But whatever great worldly entities exist that take the form of accomplishments (siddhi), [the author] says—starting with 'dravya'—that although substances and so forth grant accomplishments, they do not assist in the attainment of the state of Brahman. (28–29)

The meaning is that because there is nothing desirable for one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) apart from Brahman, he desires nothing at all. The word "iti" signifies the completion of the chapter.
Thus ends the third chapter.
The fourth chapter: 1. Brāhmaṇa.
Within the seven stages [of yoga], there are four stages of liberation while living (jīvanmukti).
Then Nidāgha asked the venerable Ṛbhu:
"Please describe the characteristics of liberation while living. "So be it," he said, and spoke concerning the seven stages.
There are four types of those liberated while living. || 2 ||

The first stage is the desire for the auspicious (*śubhecchā*); the second is investigation (*vicāraṇā*); the third is the attenuation of the mind (*tanumānasī*); the fourth is the attainment of being (*sattvāpatti*); the fifth is non-attachment (*asaṃsakti*); the sixth is the contemplation of the meaning of the words (*padārthabhāvanā*); and the seventh is that which goes beyond the fourth (*turīyagā*). || 3 ||

Desiring to know the characteristics of one liberated while living without the mind (*acittajīvanmukta*), Nidāgha asks Ṛbhu about its full extent; thus the text says: "Then... He asked—what?—"Please describe the characteristics of liberation while living. (1) To the question of what he said in response, [the text replies]: "In the seven stages... (saptabhūmiṣu).
2 || Regarding the question "What kind of stages (bhūmis) are they?", he says: "Auspicious," etc. 3 ||

The fourfold nature of the syllable Om, beginning with the letter 'a' and its modifications, consists of the stages whose essence is the syllable Om: namely, the letters 'a', 'u', 'm', and the half-measure (ardhamātrā). || 4 ||
The [objects of perception], beginning with form, are of four kinds, distinguished as gross, subtle, seed, and witness. || 5 ||
The modifications of the Praṇava, however, consist of the letters A, U, M, and the half-mora.
He states the fourfold nature of the modifications of the *praṇava*, beginning with the letter 'a', in the verse starting with "sthūla" (verse 5).

The states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (turiya) are the direct perceptions of the gross and other aspects of the letter A. In the gross aspect of the letter A, there is the waking Viśva; in its subtle aspect, that is the Taijasa; and in its seed aspect, that is the Prājña.
In its witness-aspect (sākṣyaṃśa), it is the fourth (turīya). || 7 || In the gross aspect (sthūlāṃśa) of the letter *U*, it is Viśva in the dream state;
in its subtle aspect (sūkṣmāṃśa), it is Taijasa; in its seed-aspect (bījāṃśa), it is Prājña; in its witness-aspect, it is the fourth. || 8 ||

In the gross aspect of the letter *ma*, there is the Viśva of deep sleep; in its subtle aspect, the Taijasa; in its seed-aspect, the Prājña; and in its witness-aspect, the Turya. In the gross aspect of the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*), there is the Viśva of the Fourth State (*turya*); in its subtle aspect, the Taijasa; in its seed-aspect, the Prājña; and in its witness-aspect...
The fourth of the fourth. || 10 ||
Those states which are differentiated as the letter *a* and so forth are [the phonemes]. (6)
He describes the division of their presiding deities according to the sequence beginning with the gross form of the letter *a* and so forth, starting with the phrase "The letter *a*":
the presiding deities of the collective waking-waking state and so forth range from Virāṭ and Virāṭ-Īśvara up to Turyabīja;
whereas the presiding deities of the unity of their individual and collective aspects range from Atrī and Atrī-Īśvara up to Avikalpānujñaikarasa.
These are to be understood as occurring. || 7-9 ||

It is the supreme ground, which transcends even the awakening to the impossibility of the multitude of presiding deities over the fifteen states— beginning with waking-within-waking— which are differentiated within the portions of the witness that are divided from the witness-portion itself by the subtle distinctions of the individual and collective manifestations (*vyaṣṭi-samaṣṭi-kalanā*), and which possess forms fashioned by the notions of individuality and so forth as being separate from the Self.
The meaning is that the Fourth-of-the-Fourth is victorious. || 10 ||

The distinctions of the stages (*bhūmikā*) according to the components of the *praṇava* are as follows: the first, second, and third stages are the fourth parts of the letters *a*, *u*, and *m* respectively;
the fourth stage is the fourth part of the letter *u*; and the fifth stage is the fourth part of the letter *m*.
The sixth stage consists of the first, second, and third parts, which are divided by half-mātrās;
the seventh stage transcends that. || 11 ||
In that context, the fourth parts [of the letters] beginning with *a* are present; the meaning is that the seventh stage (*bhūmikā*) transcends those.
There are four types of those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).

One who dwells in the first three stages becomes a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*); one who dwells in the fourth stage becomes a knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*); and one who dwells in the fifth stage becomes an excellent knower of Brahman (*brahmavidvara*).
Dwelling on the sixth stage, he becomes the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman; dwelling on the seventh stage, he becomes the most eminent among the knowers of Brahman. || 12 ||
Regarding how there is a fourfold division of those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), it is stated: "In the three stages" (*bhūmitrayeṣu*). || 12 ||
p. 494) 2. The Mantra: The Exposition of the Seven Stages. In this regard, there are these verses:
The first stage of knowledge is declared to be *śubhecchā* (the desire for virtue);
the second is *vicāraṇā* (investigation), and the third is *tanumānasī* (the thinning of the mind). || 1 ||

The fourth is the attainment of being (sattvāpatti); after that is the one named non-attachment (asaṃsakti). The sixth is the contemplation on the nature of reality (padārthabhāvanā), and the seventh is remembered as the state beyond the fourth (turyagā). || 2 ||
In this regard, he shows the restatement of the collection of mantras: "In that context, these verses occur.
Thus, the names of the stages have been stated in brief. (1–2)
"Am I indeed still deluded while standing here? I must be examined by the learned and the virtuous.
Desiring this first with dispassion is called *śubhecchā* (the desire for the auspicious) by the wise. (3)
That engagement in virtuous conduct which is preceded by the study of the scriptures, association with the wise, and the practice of dispassion is called *vicāraṇā* (investigation).
Where attachment to the objects of the senses is attenuated through both investigation and virtuous aspiration,
that state is called *tanumānasī*.
Through the practice of the three stages, by virtue of the mind's withdrawal from objects,
when it abides in the pure self of *sattva*, that is declared to be the attainment of *sattva*.

That [state] which results from the practice of the four stages and has non-attachment as its fruit, in which the wonder of pure being (*sattva*) is firmly rooted, is called *asaṃsakti* (non-attachment). (7)
Through the intense practice of the five stages, by virtue of delighting solely in one's own self, there arises a non-contemplation of internal and external objects. (8)
The sixth stage is called the contemplation of the meaning of the words (padārthabhāvanā), which consists in awakening through prolonged effort prompted by another.
Due to long-term practice on the six stages and because no differentiation is perceived,
that state of being solely established in one's own nature is to be known as the fourth stage of realization.
He states their characteristics: "Established," etc.
These seven stages, beginning with *śubhecchā*, have been explained for the most part in the *Mahadannapūrṇākṣy-upaniṣads*. (3–17)
An examination of the distinctions in the states of the intellect across the seven stages:
the triad beginning with *śubhecchā* is known to be endowed with both distinctions and non-distinctions of the stages.
One who perceives this world as it truly is through the intellect sees it as a waking state. (11)
When non-duality has attained stability and duality has come to rest,
they perceive the world like a dream through the excellent yoga of the fourth stage (turya).
Like the dissolution of fragments of autumn clouds, it dissolves away;
O Nidāgha, remain as that which consists of pure being alone—make this firm.
Having ascended the fifth stage, known as the state of deep sleep,
he remains in that which is pure non-duality, wherein all particularities have been stilled.
Though constantly intent on external activity due to its inward-facing nature, it always appears as if drowsy because of its perpetual exhaustion. (15)
Practicing on this stage and completely eliminating [the afflictions], one reaches the ancient seventh stage, known as "Deep Sleep. (16)

Where there is neither the form of non-existence nor existence, neither "I" nor even the absence of egoism—one remains solely in non-duality, utterly fearless, with all mental constructions extinguished. (17)
The method of contemplating the nature of the self as the absolute Brahman is like an empty jar in the sky—empty within and empty without;
yet it is like a full jar in the ocean—full within and full without. (18)
Do not become the nature of the grasped object, and do not become the nature of the grasper; having abandoned all mental constructions, become absorbed in that which remains. (19)
Having abandoned the seer, the seeing, and the seen, along with all latent impressions,
resort to the Self alone, which is the primordial manifestation of seeing.
He says, "O Nidāgha, worship Brahman— which is devoid of internal and external conceptualization— as your own non-dual self alone," in the verse beginning with "antar" (18).

The meaning is: "May that which is the object of perception—the entire collection of distinctions imagined by the mind—and that which is the mental subject perceiving it, may both of these not come to be. (19) The passage beginning with "empty within" and ending with "worship [Him] alone" has been explained in the Maitreyopaniṣad. (20)
He for whom this world, as it exists, has set like the sky— remaining yet vanished even while engaged in worldly activity— is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 21 ||
The radiance of the mind neither rises nor sets in pleasure or pain;
he whose state remains exactly as it is attained is called one liberated while living. (22)
He who remains awake while established in deep sleep, for whom no waking state exists, and whose consciousness is free from latent impressions—he is called one liberated while living. (23)
Even while acting in accordance with passion, aversion, fear, and the like, he who is as utterly transparent as the inner sky is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 24 ||
He whose state of being is free from egoism, whose intellect is not defiled—
whether he is acting or not acting— he is called liberated while living.
He from whom the world does not shrink away, and who does not shrink away from the world, being liberated from joy, envy, and fear—he is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 26 ||
He who, though engaged in the entire web of worldly affairs, remains cool and whose self is as full as it is in the pursuit of others' welfare—he is called one liberated while living. (27)
O Sage, when one abandons all desires residing in the mind and finds contentment in Me, who am the Self of all, he is called liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 28 ||
He whose mind is undisturbed and who rests in that supremely purifying state of pure consciousness, devoid of the notion of a shrine (caitya), is called liberated while living. (29)
He in whose mind this world, this "I," and this entire collection of visible objects—which are unreal—no longer manifests, is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 30 ||
It has been stated that there are four types of those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). He states their characteristics, beginning with "Just as," and so forth:
just as the sky remains exactly as it is, whether pots, bowls, and the like exist or do not exist, so too it is for him.

(498) Even for one who has become silent and is engaged in worldly activity, when the mind has either set or remains within the three states such as deep sleep, it becomes focused solely upon Brahman; such a person is called liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 21 || Furthermore—“It does not arise” || 22 || Furthermore—“He who is awake” || 23–26.
He is cool because of the absence of internal feverish distress. (27–30)
The rule for steadfastness in Brahman: having quickly entered that vast, full, and objectless True Brahman which is stable, through the path of the teacher and the scriptures, become firm. 31.
Śiva is the Guru, Śiva is the Veda, Śiva is the God, Śiva is the Lord;
I am Śiva, all is Śiva, there is nothing other than Śiva.
Having understood that very [Self], the wise Brahmin should cultivate wisdom;
he should not contemplate many words, for that is a weariness of speech. (33)

"You too, O Nidāgha, having entered into the True Brahman—the Infinite Brahman which is pure Being—by means of the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher, become instantly firm; that is to say, take refuge in the state of being that alone. As to what the nature of this Self of expansive bliss is, he says: "Śiva."
32 || He who, having swallowed the inauspiciousness that is other than Himself, remains as His own self alone—of Him it has been explained in this *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*. 33 ||
The bird, the ant, the discernment of the path, Śuka was liberated, and Vāmadeva was also liberated; apart from these, there are none who possess liberation.
Those wise ones who follow the path of Śuka become liberated in this very world.
Those who constantly follow Vāmadeva, dying and being born again and again therein,
indeed become those liberated by gradual progression in this world.
By means of yoga, Sāṃkhya, ritual actions, and those endowed with devotion. || 35 ||
Śuka and Vāmadeva are the two paths ordained by the gods;
Śuka is said to be the bird, and Vāmadeva is the ant.

Either by way of the exclusion of what is not that (*atadvyāvṛtti*), or directly through the positive mode (*vidhimukha*), [one attains it] through inquiry into the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*) and through the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of Sāṃkhya and Yoga. || 37 ||
Having realized the nature of their own self through asamprajñāta-samādhi,
those free from passion proceed by way of Śukra to the supreme state.

Through the forceful practice of the postures, such as Yama and the rest, performed again and again, one who has encountered a multitude of obstacles may, by virtue of powers such as *aṇimā*, [attain results] in this very life. (39)
Even if he does not attain the fruit correctly, having been born again into a great family,
he will once more practice the yoga through his former latent impressions alone.
Indeed, by means of the path of Vāmadeva through practice over many births,
he too attains liberation— that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
These two paths are both auspicious and lead to the attainment of Brahman:
one bestows immediate liberation, and the other bestows gradual liberation.
(500) Now, one might object: "Śuka is liberated and Vāmadeva is also liberated"—by this, only two become liberated.

Indeed, a third cannot be reckoned as liberated along with those two. If that were the case, for what purpose would there be the performance of obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*) and so forth, the means of purification of the mind, and the fourfold requirements for renunciation (*sannyāsa*) in the world?

If it be argued that their efforts are not likely to bear fruit, we say no; for the scriptural statements, "Śuka was liberated" and "Vāmadeva was also liberated," have another purpose, namely, they refer to the paths taken by birds and ants. Therefore, engagement in the means of knowledge is fruitful.
To this he says: "Śuka. Śuka, following the path of birds, becomes liberated immediately (*sadyo-mukta*).

Vāmadeva, even though following the path of ants, becomes liberated gradually (*krama-mukta*). Beyond these two paths, there are indeed no others who possess liberation; for this purpose, [the text] is made perfectly clear.
The Śruti itself reveals this: "Śuka," thus [it says]. (34–36)
He states the means for attaining the path of Śuka: "Not this" (atad), etc. [Verse 37-38].

Either by way of direct affirmation—namely, that Brahman is one's own self alone, devoid of any counter-correlate, established through the impossibility of any conception of what is other than itself by means of the form of exclusion as "not this, not this" (neti neti) and "for not from this" (na hy etasmāt)—or [by way of negation], [the path is attained].

He states the essential nature of the path of Vāmadeva: "yamā... (vv. 39–40). He also attains liberation gradually: "...so'pi muktiṃ krameṇa samāpnoti" (v. 41). He states the established meaning: "dvāv... (v. 42).

The expansion of the vision of one who knows Brahman possesses such purity that for him who perceives oneness, what delusion can there be, and what sorrow? This is so for one whose intellect, reaching the limit of direct experience, proceeds toward reality. (43)
All those who come within the range of his vision are liberated from all sins;
all beings, whether moving in the sky or moving on the earth, are freed when they come within the range of the vision of one who knows Brahman.
They are immediately liberated from the sins accumulated over ten million births.
Thus it is said.
The state that is attained by the followers of Sāṃkhya is also reached by the practitioners of Yoga;
he who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one truly sees.

(p. 501) According to the Smṛti, the meaning is that the two paths culminate in the unity of the fruits to be attained; thus, the word "there" (*tatra*) is used. He says, "of whom," to show that even one who is purified by the vision of such a knower is liberated from the inauspicious. Whatever the knower of Brahman perceives as separate from himself—

He does not perceive anything other than that respective Brahman. By the power of his merit, those purified by his vision become ones who have accomplished all that was to be done; this is the meaning. The word "iti" signifies the conclusion of the chapter.
Thus ends the fourth chapter.
The fifth chapter:
For one who desires yoga, knowledge of the body is essential.
Then Nidāgha asked the venerable Ṛbhu:
"Please explain the method for the practice of yoga. "So be it," he said, and spoke as follows:
"The body consists of the five elements and is filled with the five spheres (maṇḍalas)."
Solidity is the earth alone; this water has the form of fluidity. (1)
Luminosity is the characteristic of fire, and movement is the characteristic of wind;
all of space arises from sattva—all this should be known by one who desires yoga. (2)

Having correctly understood from the mouth of his teacher the characteristics of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), Nidāgha [inquired] regarding the practice of yoga, which serves as the means for the knowledge of non-dual Brahman—the cause of liberation while living.
[The teacher], accepting Nidāgha’s question, said, "So be it. He then spoke.
Since the practice of yoga is accomplished by means of the body, he states the extent of the body in the verse beginning with "five" (*pañca*).
To the question of how the body consists of the five elements, he says: "solidity" (*kāṭhinya*) and so forth. (1–2)
The number of breaths here is twenty-one thousand six hundred;
by means of these breaths flowing during a day and night, one destroys the wind-mandala. (3)
Regarding the question of how many breaths are completed in a day and night, he says: "Six," etc. (Verse 3).
The method for sustaining the elements in order to prevent the decay of the body:
when that earthly element (pṛthvī) within the body diminishes, wrinkles appear upon embodied beings;
likewise, upon the depletion of the group of waters (āpaḥ), the hair gradually becomes white.

When the fire-element (tejas) diminishes, hunger destroys the luster; when the wind-element (māruta) diminishes, trembling constantly arises, and one does not live at all without the ether-element (nābhasa).
Thus, because of the constant depletion [of the elements], life—which is the support of the elements—[comes to an end].

As long as the portions of the five elements that constitute the body are not exhausted, the body remains intact; but upon their exhaustion, it undergoes transformation. He says "that" (tad) [to explain this]: when the *nābhasa* [element] is exhausted, [the body perishes]. (5)
Since the body perishes through the depletion of the elements, the meaning is that one must constantly maintain those respective elements for the sake of the body's life.
The practice of the uḍḍiyāṇabandha is for the purpose of supporting the vital elements (bhūta), because by means of it, the great bird [of the breath] flies without rest. (6)
That very [place] is Uḍḍiyāṇa; the binding there is what is called the Uḍḍiyāṇa-bandha.
Indeed, this Uḍḍiyāṇa-bandha is a lion to the elephant of death. (7)
The enjoyment of that [food] occurs from the body; indeed, its binding within the body is difficult to accomplish.
When the fire moves within the belly, intense pain arises. (8)
It should not be performed even when one is hungry, nor when one is pressed by the urge of feces or urine.
One should eat what is wholesome and moderate, in small quantities and many times.

He describes the *uḍyāṇabandha*, which is conducive to the retention of the vital elements (*bhūtadhāraṇā*), with the words "the *uḍyāṇa*" (verse 6–7). Liberation from that *uḍyāṇabandha* occurs through the body, due to the firmness of the body.
Because it cannot be performed at all times, it is difficult to practice. Regarding its constant performance, what [is the result]?
Regarding the point that this leads to loss, he says: "In the case of fire" (verse 8). One should eat what is wholesome and moderate for the sake of allaying hunger (verse 9).
The three yogas known as laya, mantra, and haṭha correspond respectively to the mild, middling, and intense types of mantras;
these are mantra, laya, and haṭha yoga, which is indeed endowed with eight limbs.
Having thus pacified hunger, one should practice yoga; so he says: "Gentle," etc.
"Gentle" refers to *laya* (absorption), "middling" to *haṭha*, and "mantra" to the contemplation of *nāda* (the primordial sound), because *nāda* is the root of all mantras. Among these—

In the mild and middling mantras, one should know that the sequence consists of the mantra, the contemplation of the sound (nāda), then dissolution (laya), and its means, which is Haṭha. Among these, the mantra is the cause of dissolution, and Haṭha is the cause of that [mantra]. Thus, the yogas are of three kinds. Therein, the first is Haṭhayoga.
The meaning is that he becomes endowed with the eight limbs of self-restraint (yama) today. || 10 ||
The eight limbs of yoga are: restraint (yama), observance (niyama), and likewise posture (āsana);
then breath control (prāṇāyāma), and thereafter withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra). || 11 ||
Retention (*dhāraṇā*), as well as meditation (*dhyāna*), and concentration (*samādhi*) shall be the eighth.
To the question "What are the eight limbs of yoga?", he says: "And restraint" (*yamaśca*), etc. (11).
The divisions of the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama) are: non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, and straightforwardness. || 12 ||
Forbearance, fortitude, moderation in diet, and purity—these are the ten *yamas*.
Austerity, contentment, faith, charity, and worship of the Lord [are the five *niyamas*]. (13)
Listening to the established doctrine, modesty, intelligence, recitation, and vows—these, O high-minded one, are declared to be the tenfold observances (niyamas). 14.
In brief, he indicates the names of the eight limbs beginning with restraint: "non-violence," and so forth (12–16).
O best of sages, there are eleven seats, beginning with the discus;
they are the discus, the lotus seat, the tortoise, the peacock, and likewise the cock. (15)
Vīrāsana, Svastika, Bhadra, Siṃhāsana, as well as Muktāsana and Gomukha, have been proclaimed by those most skilled in yoga. (16)
The characteristic of the wheel posture (*cakrāsana*):
one should place the left thigh upon the right ankle and the right [thigh] upon the other [left ankle], while keeping the body straight; this is considered the wheel posture. (17)
In that regard, he states the characteristics of the wheel-seat (cakrāsana): "The left... (verse 17).

Breath control (prāṇāyāma) consists of inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and likewise exhalation (recaka); since these are performed again and again through one's own channels (nāḍīs), they are therefore called "channels. (18)
The practices of non-violence and the rest, as divided according to Yama and so forth, are to be applied in accordance with the method of the *darśana* (philosophical systems) and the *upaniṣads*.
Now, he describes *prāṇāyāma*: "Pūraka," etc. (Verse 18).
Regarding the measurements of the body and its parts:
the body of all living beings consists of ninety-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
In the middle of that, two finger-breadths beyond the region of the anus is the supreme [seat]. (19)
Two finger-breadths below the region of the penis is called the center;
nine finger-breadths above the penis is called the bulb (kanda) of the channels.
Four fingers in height and four fingers in length, egg-shaped, and enveloped by fat, marrow, bone, and blood. (21)
Now, having first explained the measurement of the body, he analyzes the network of channels (nāḍīcakra) with the words: "The body... and so forth.
The wheel of channels (nāḍīcakra) is located right there; indeed, the twelve-spoked wheel of channels is established.
By means of it the body is sustained, and therein the Kuṇḍalinī abides.
That Suṣumnā which reaches the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) covers it with its mouth;
the Alambusā and the Kuhū nāḍī reside within that Suṣumnā.
In the pair of spokes immediately following, Vāruṇā and Yaśasvinī are located;
then, on the southern spoke, Piṅgalā follows Suṣumnā in sequence.
Between those two, Pūṣan exists as the milch-cow;
and in the western movement, the Sarasvatī channel is situated as Suṣumnā. (25)
Śaṅkhinī and Gāndhārī are situated immediately after those two;
to the north of Suṣumṇā, however, dwells that one called Iḍā.
Immediately following that is Hastijihvā, and then Viśvodarī is situated;
thus, in a clockwise sequence, these are the channels (nāḍīs) upon the spokes of the wheel.
Indeed, these twelve exist as the carriers of the twelve winds;
the channels (nāḍīs) are described as being of various colors, situated like a cloth. || 28 ||
The place in the middle of the cloth is called the navel-cakra;
it is declared to be the support of the sound (nāda), blazing and having the form of sound. (29)
The *pararandhra* and the *suṣumnā*, these four are filled with jewels;
the center of the *brahmarandhra* is perpetually covered by the *kuṇḍalī*.
In this way, the ten vital winds (vāyu) move within these channels.
"Between those two" means in the middle of the two petals situated therein. (25–32)
The method for practicing the vision of the Fourth State (turiya):
Thus, having understood the movement of the channels and the movement of the vital breath, the wise one— || 31 ||
With neck, head, and body held straight, the mouth closed, and perfectly motionless;
[one should fix the mind] on the tip of the nose, in the center of the heart, and in the center of the *bindu* for the fourth state.

With a well-concentrated mind, one should behold the flowing nectar with both eyes. (p. 507) Yoga, which serves as the means for deceiving death, consists of closing the anus and drawing up the *apāna* wind so that it faces upward. || 33 ||
Having raised [the self] with the Praṇava, one should withdraw it with the Śrībīja;
then one should meditate upon oneself as Śrī, followed by the immersion in nectar.
This is indeed declared to be the foremost of all methods for cheating death:
that by which an action conceived in the mind is accomplished by means of the mind alone. (35)
Indeed, from the blazing of fire upon water, branches and sprouts do arise;
for no word uttered by a person of merit can have an contrary effect. (36)
He states the means for deceiving death: "Apānam" (verse 33).

Having raised the *apāna* upward by means of the syllable *praṇava*, and having turned the *prāṇa* downward by means of the *śrībīja*, one should contemplate one's own self—situated at the junction of the *apāna* and *prāṇa*—as the glory of liberation (*muktiśrī*).

Then one should perform the immersion in nectar (*amṛtaplāvana*) and the consecration with nectar (*amṛtābhiṣecana*). (34) That which has been described is indeed the deception of time (*kālavañcana*) and the stabilization of life-force (*āyuḥstambhana*); they declare that very thing to be the primary [practice] for yogins.
He states the fruit of the yoga of deceiving time with the words beginning "with the mind" (*manasā*). (35) What kind of perfection (*siddhi*) is accomplished?
In this context, "in water" means: whatever has been stated therein is not without merit. || 36 ||

The yogas that serve as the means for achieving physical firmness, strength, and so forth, consist in binding the *bindu* at the path, igniting the fire within the vital breath (*jīvana*), and drying up the water; by this, the body becomes firm. (37)
One should contract the anus and the perineum simultaneously; having caused the apāna wind to move upward, one should join it with the samāna wind. || 38 ||
Then, the yogin should meditate upon his own self as Śrī, flooded with nectar; thereafter, he should exert his power from the region of the middle door. (39)
One should practice meditation for the sake of ascending, through the excellent union of prāṇa and apāna;
this is the supreme yoga within the body that illuminates the path to perfection. 40.

Having fixed the mental *bindu* on the path of the *suṣumnā*, one should, by means of contraction, ignite the wind located there at the *mūlādhāra* within the life-force (*jīvana*). Then, with that fire accompanied by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), one should dry up the fatty substance (*vasā*) situated within the *suṣumnā* channel and arrest the vital breaths and so forth. By that—
The meaning is that the yogi shall possess a firm body. (37) He states the supreme yoga that produces strength, beginning with "guda" (the anus):

simultaneously contracting both the anus and the *yoni*, and then raising the *apāna* upward, joining it with the *samāna*. (38) [One should contemplate] the Self as the substratum for the junction of *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and *samāna*.

Having meditated upon Jñānaśrī and consecrated him with nectar, the yogin should begin the *kumbhaka* (retention of breath) according to his strength from the middle gate-section. Then, through the excellent union of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, he should contemplate the *prāṇa* together with *udāna* for the sake of its upward movement; this is precisely the practice that has been described.
This supreme yoga becomes an indicator of the path to perfection within the body; the meaning is that this yoga leads to the attainment of the world of Brahman. || 40 ||
The method for knowing the shadow of the body:
Just as a dam built across water obstructs the flow, so too must the shadow residing within the body be constantly understood by yogis. (41)
He states that one's own bodily shadow must be known in order to know the time of the body's end,

beginning with the words "Just as" (yathā). Just as a stone dam situated in a river acts as an obstruction to the current, so too does the reflection of consciousness (cicchāyā) within the body— the power of the individual soul (jīvaśakti)— having set aside the portion of power residing therein [in the heart].

The supreme consciousness, non-different from the inner self, should always be known by yogis as "I am the Self, non-different from the inner self. Thereupon, having become a knower of time whose locus is the cessation of identification with the body, one remains in the form of the Self that is Time. This is the bridge of yoga consisting of the power of consciousness.
The meaning is that he becomes one who obstructs the outward flow [of the breath]. || 41 ||
The method for binding the crossroads is the *saṃpuṭayoga*;
this is proclaimed to be the binding of all the channels (*nāḍī*) indeed.
By the grace of this binding, the deity becomes manifest. (42)
This is the fourfold junction of bonds that obstructs the three paths;
it opens up the single path by which the perfected ones have attained perfect union. (43)
Having made the udāna rise upward together with the prāṇa by means of force, this binding of all the channels goes upward, bringing about cessation. (44)
This is the Saṃpuṭa-yoga, and it is also considered the Mūla-bandha;
by the practice of this very yoga, the triad of bandhas is accomplished. (45)
He speaks of the yoga of the *saṃpuṭa* (encasement) as a means for binding at the crossroads—beginning with the words "of all" (*sarvāsām*).
This [yoga] which is about to be described pertains to "all. To the question "What would happen by this?", he says "of the binding" (*bandhasya*).
The meaning is that the deity, which is the inward-facing consciousness, shines forth. Furthermore—regarding the word "this" (*eṣa*)—where...

The channels Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Kuhū attain unity; this is the fourfold path, the four-gated [center] which has its locus in the Mūlādhāra. Therein lies the "root-lock" (mūlabandha), which consists of constant contraction. There, by means of that entry into the aperture of the Suṣumṇā, one becomes perfected (siddhā).
Expanding that single path called Suṣumṇā, one attains the perfection characterized by the state of Brahman;
one becomes the obstructer of the three pathways situated within the channels of Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Kuhū.
By the word "Kuhū," the cavity of the Apāna is meant. (43) He describes the method for doing so:

Regarding the term *udāna*: by means of yogic practice, having caused the *udāna* breath to move upward along with the *prāṇa* through force, and having applied the *mūlabandha* and *jālandhara*, this *bandha* shines like a casket, acting as a blockage of the paths of all the *nāḍīs*. At that time, the *prāṇa*...

That which proceeds upward through the path of the *suṣumnā* to the thousand-petalled wheel (*sahasrāra*) together with the *kuṇḍalinī*, the mind-vision, and the fire—this is called the "enveloping" (*saṃpuṭa*) yoga.
The meaning is that this very [practice] is also the *mūlabandha*. Thus, by means of this *saṃpuṭa* yoga through the practice of cultivation...
The three bonds are also accomplished. || 45 ||
p. 510) The sequence for attaining the knowledge of Brahman through the practice of *saṃpuṭa*:
"Day and night, without interruption, at every watch—whenever that may be—by this yoga of practice, the vital wind (*vāyu*) becomes mastered. (46)
When the wind is practiced, the digestive fire increases in the body day by day;
and as the fire grows stronger, food and other sustenance are easily digested. (47)
Through the digestion of food, the increase of the nutrient essence (rasa) arises;
when the essence has increased, the bodily constituents (dhātus) likewise constantly grow. (48)
By the very increase of the elements, awakening increases within the body;
all sins accumulated over ten million births are consumed by fire. (49)

The meaning is that whenever this may be—whether day or night, or even in every watch—one’s vital breath (prāṇa) becomes practiced through this yoga of repetition. By means of this practice, the knowledge of Brahman also gradually manifests; thus he says: "In the air," etc. (verses 47–48).
Upon the destruction of all sins without remainder, the knowledge of the non-dual Brahman arises in the form "I am Brahman.
The meaning is that at that very moment, the knower becomes liberated. || 49 ||
The Description of the Abode of Śiva and Śakti:
Situated between the anus and the genitals is the Mūlādhāra, which is triangular;
it is indeed the abode of Śiva in the form of the Bindu, and it is illuminating. (50)
Therein is established the supreme power named Kuṇḍalinī, from which wind arises and from which fire increases. (51)
From which the *bindu* arises, from which the *nāda* increases, from which the *haṃsa* is produced, and from which the mind (*manas*) is produced. || 52 ||
The six cakras beginning with the mūlādhāra are declared to be the abode of Śakti;
from the throat up to the crown of the head is called the abode of Śambhu. (53)
He explains the nature of Śiva and Śakti, beginning with the words "guda" (verse 50) up to verse 53.

Prāṇāyāma accompanied by the contemplation of Brahman is the support of the channels (nāḍīs); the body is the support of the channels, and the vital breath (prāṇa) is the abode of the individual soul (jīva); the individual soul, in turn, is the support of the Haṃsa. (54)
The *haṃsa* is the substratum of *śakti*, and this entire world, both moving and unmoving, is it.
Free from conceptual construction and with a serene mind, one should practice *prāṇāyāma*. (55)

Even while abiding in the three correct bonds, one whose mind is fixed on the commitment to truth should constantly extract the object of knowledge— the cause characterized by its defining marks— from the realm of the knowable.
One should restrain both exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka) within the retention (kumbhaka),
while resting of one's own accord in the Supreme Brahman, which is the visible goal.
The exhaling breath (recaka) is declared to be all objects situated within one's own mind;
the inhaling breath (pūraka) is the knowledge of the scriptures, and the retention breath (kumbhaka) is remembered as that which is established in the Self.
If one’s mind is thus practiced, one is liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Having always raised [the breath] by means of *kumbhaka*, one should fill it by means of *kumbhaka* alone. (59)
One should fill the *kumbha* with the *kumbha*, [visualizing] the supreme Śiva residing within it;
then, one should strike firmly today with the *kaṇṭhamudrā*. (60)

Having obstructed the movement of the winds and having performed inhalation (pūraka) and retention (kumbhaka), one should practice prāṇāyāma with this understanding; thus he says: "Of the channels... (verse 54).
The *haṃsa*—the Supreme Self non-different from the inner self—is the substratum of power (*śakti*).

The entire world of moving and non-moving beings is indeed the effect of the power of *māyā*. (55) Thus, he says "perfectly" (*samyak*) to explain that the yogi, endowed with the aforementioned means, becomes liberated from the delusion of anything other than his own self.

Though firmly established in the three bandhas through the piercing of Mūlādhāra, Uḍḍiyāṇa, and Jālandhara, one realizes the object of knowledge—the oneness of the inner self and Brahman (56). [This is achieved through] recaka, whose characteristics will be described hereafter (57).
The meaning is that the very contemplation of one's own true nature (*svasvarūpānusaṃdhāna*)— which has as its object the internal sphere imagined by one's own ignorance—
is *kumbhaka*. By means of such *kumbhaka*,
one performs only the pure *kumbhaka* (without inhalation or exhalation), preceded by the contemplation of the nature of Brahman.

The meaning is that one should do this always. (59) If the mind should go outward, then one should strike it back again. If, due to the practice of *kevala-kumbhaka*, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) goes out along with its own retinue, then by means of the throat-mudrā called *jālandhara-bandha*, one should ensure that it becomes well-stabilized.

Having obstructed and overcome the upward and downward movement of the vital airs (vāyu), and having again maintained the inhalation (pūraka) and retention (kumbhaka), one should strike; that is to say, one should practice it. || 60 ||
The sequence for practicing the yoga of piercing is as follows:
the pair of hands should be level on the ground, and likewise the pair of feet. || 61 ||
By means of the conjunction of the three piercing [breaths], one should strike the four seats with the wind;
one should strike the great Meru with millions of blows from the mouth of the wind.
Having drawn in both nostrils equally, the breath vibrates rapidly;
through the connection with the moon, sun, and fire, one should know this indeed leads to immortality.
The gods situated in the center of Meru tremble due to the shaking of Meru;
first, the piercing [of the central channel] quickly arises for him from the Brahma-knot. (64)
Then, having pierced the Brahma-knot, he pierces the Viṣṇu-knot;
then, having pierced the Viṣṇu-knot, he pierces the Rudra-knot.
Then, having pierced the Rudra-knot and likewise severed the impurity of delusion, through the grace of the Guru and the Deity resulting from the impressions of many births; || 66 ||
Then, from the practice of yoga, piercing occurs for that yogi in the circle of the *suṣumnā* channel between the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*.

By means of a specific binding of the *mudrā*, one should cause the vital air (*vāyu*) to move upward. Thus he describes the sequence for practicing the yoga of piercing (*vedhaka-yoga*): "Evenly," etc.
The yogi, having ascended to the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) on level ground within his yoga-shed, should keep the pair of hands and feet even.

Having thus become motionless, one should pierce the knots of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra with the life-force (*prāṇavāyu*) together with its attendants; in this way, through the application of the three piercing agents,
[one should awaken] the *prāṇakuṇḍalinī* at the mouth of the *suṣumnā* with the tips of the rays by means of its own attendants.

Having reached that, one should strike—that is, one should cause to resound—the consciousness of the fourfold throne of the thousand-spoked wheel, which is situated above it, with the thought "I am [that]";
the meaning is that one should meditate upon it as being all-pervasive. What follows from this? When—

When the vital breath (prāṇa) rapidly vibrates after having drawn in and swallowed the nectar produced from the two cavities of the moon, sun, and kuṇḍalī-fire— resulting from the conjunction of the moon, sun, and fire above the three peaks known as the space between the eyebrows— then it is for the sake of nectar, that is, for immortality itself.

The meaning is that one should know that the manifestation of the dissolution of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth occurs. || 63 || Viśva, Virāṭ, Otrā, and others—whether they be Brahmā and the other deities—reside within Meru, which consists of the immutable consciousness (kūṭastha-caitanya). When the specific portions superimposed upon Meru are moved—that is, when they are reduced to the state of being devoid of distinctions—they too move, becoming devoid of distinctions.

The meaning is that they come into being. Since the realization of the immutable one situated at the thousand-spoked [cakra] is preceded by the piercing of the three knots, he describes the manner of piercing those three knots, beginning with the words "In the beginning" (ādau). Of this... [in the beginning].

p. 514) For the yogin, the piercing—that is, the breaking—of the *brahmagranthi* occurs from [the previous stage]. 64–65. Then, having successively pierced the triad of knots beginning with the *brahmagranthi* as well as the impurity of one's own ignorance, and having realized that "nothing exists apart from Brahman," simultaneously with that knowledge—

The meaning is that one becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done (*kṛtakṛtya*). Thus, he praises the piercing-yoga (*vedhakayoga*) which bestows liberation with the verse beginning "aneka" (verse 66).

The means for attaining the perfection of piercing (*vedha*)—which is obtained through the grace of a teacher and the sacred learning acquired through the well-performed merits of infinite millions of births—is as follows: "In the circle of the *suṣumnā* channel, which shines between the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*," and so forth. [This occurs] by means of the movement of the vital air (*vāyu*) within the *suṣumnā*.
The meaning is that piercing occurs as characterized by the definition previously stated.
The recitation of the Praṇava for the pacification of obstacles: the short form burns away sins, while the long form bestows liberation. || 68 ||
Through the threefold mode of utterance, it is either nourishing or overflowing;
it should be unbroken like a stream of oil and like the resonance of a long-sounding bell. (69)

He who knows that which is inexpressible at the tip of the *praṇava* is a knower of the Veda. The short [vowel] resides in the *bindu*, the long in the *brahmarandhra*, and the protracted (*pluta*) reaches the end of the twelve; this is the mantra for the attainment of grace for the sake of mantra-perfection.
This *praṇava* removes all obstacles and destroys all defects.
For the sake of pacifying the obstacles to the attainment of the *ūrdhvayoga*— which consists of the piercing (*vedha*), the means (*upāya*), and the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—
one should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the *praṇava*, which consists of four measures (*mātrā*), preceded by concentration (*dhāraṇā*) upon the supreme object of focus of the *praṇava*.
He says that one should do so—namely, "short" (hrasva). Through the recitation of the *praṇava* with a single measure (*mātrā*), the destruction of sin occurs.

68. The *praṇava* consisting of two measures (*mātrā*) is named *āpyāyana*; through its recitation, one attains prosperity (*śrī*). That which consists of three measures is "long" (*dīrgha*), or that which consists of four measures is "protracted" (*pluta*); these grant liberation.
Thus, by means of these three modes of pronunciation, one enjoys the aforementioned fruit. In this regard—

For it is stated in the Śruti: "If it is short (hrasvā), it burns away all evil and one attains immortality; if it is long (dīrghā), one attains great prosperity and attains immortality; if it is protracted (plutā), one becomes possessed of knowledge and attains immortality. (69) Because:

Thus, he says that the practice of the *praṇava* should be performed in this manner: "The short [vowel]," etc. That which resides in the *bindu* is located in the heart; that which resides at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths] is located in the upper portion of the *brahmarandhra*.
Know it to be *prasāda*, the bestower of grace. (70) Therefore, "all," etc. It is the destroyer of all defects.
The meaning is that it comes to be.
The four stages of yoga, beginning with the stage of commencement, are: commencement, the pot, as well as familiarization, and likewise [the final stage]. (71)
And "accomplishment" (niṣpatti) is thus declared; these are its four stages.
Abandoning external action produced by the three instruments [of body, speech, and mind], || 72 ||
One performs the intermediate action where the commencement is said to take place;
the wind, performing the piercing from behind, fills [the vessel] and makes it very firm. (73)
Where that [state] abides, it is called the stage known as the "Jar" (Ghaṭa) by the wise.
Where the vital breath remains motionless within the body, neither living nor lifeless,
and where the wind becomes steady in the ether— that indeed is the stage of Accumulation (Pracaya).

That stage where one who has attained the state of liberation-in-life performs the innate yoga, wherein both creation and dissolution are centered within the self— this is the stage of perfection (niṣpattibhūmikā).
Thus.

p. 516) Thus, for one whose inner self has been purified by the repetition of the *praṇava*, he describes the four stages of yoga (*yogabhūmikā*) as the means to the yoga of the Great Piercing (*mahāvedhaka*): "And the beginning," etc. (71).
Regarding that, he states the characteristic of the stage of commencement (*ārambhabhūmikā*): "By means of the instruments" (*karaṇa*), etc.
[Verse 72]. It is produced by the three instruments known as mind, speech, and body. He describes the second stage:
"In whatever manner it occurs, while piercing the three knots (*granthi*), wherever one remains—that is this [stage]."

The meaning is that it becomes the stage of the jar (*ghaṭabhūmikā*). He states the definition of the stage of accumulation (*pracayabhūmikā*) with the words "not that" (*na sā*): because of the absence of movement, it is not "with life" (*sajīva*); because of the presence of vital breath (*prāṇa*), it is not "lifeless" (*nirjīva*). That in which the wind becomes steady within the space of the thousand-spoked wheel (*sahasrāra*)—this is the stage of accumulation; such is the meaning. || 74 ||
He states the characteristic of the stage of accomplishment (*niṣpattibhūmikā*) with the words "wherein" (*yatra*). In that fourth stage,
the yogi, having become the Self of Īśvara and having performed the creation and dissolution of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) such as waking and so forth,
attains the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) and practices the innate yoga known as *asaṃprajñāta*.
This is the stage of accomplishment (niṣpattibhūmikā). The word "iti" signifies the completion of the four stages.
This is the fruit of studying and understanding this Vidyā.
Whoever studies this Upaniṣad becomes purified by fire; he becomes purified by wind;
he becomes purified from the drinking of liquor; he becomes purified from the theft of gold; he becomes liberated while living. 76

This very thing has been declared by a Ṛgvedic verse: "The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, like an eye extended in the sky. The inspired poets, ever-watchful and praising, kindle that which is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. Thus ends the Upaniṣad.
He states the fruit of reciting this knowledge with the words "etad" (this). Whoever studies this Upaniṣad—He states the fruit of that knowledge: "he is liberated while living" (jīvanmukta). || 76 ||
This mantra is explained in the Āruṇika Upaniṣad. Thus, the word "Upaniṣad" serves to mark the conclusion of the Varāha Upaniṣad. || 77 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter. The commentary on the Varāhopaniṣad, which has Brahman as its object, has been written by Upaniṣadbrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra.
The collection of commentaries on the Varāhopaniṣad consists of four hundred works.
Thus ends the commentary on the Varāhopaniṣad, completing the ninety-eighth [treatise] in the venerable exposition of the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the Īśa.
